Title: PhD positions in Biology at the University of Texas at Arlington (Dallas-Fort Worth, Texas)
 Description: 
The Department of Biology at the University of Texas at Arlington (UTA) is recruiting doctoral students for Fall 2027. All PhD students are guaranteed a full five years of funding, including salary, tuition, and healthcare.
 
Our department spans a wide range of cutting-edge topics and techniques in biological research, with research areas including cell and developmental biology, microbiology, genomics, and ecology and evolution. Our PhD program focuses on training students to apply sophisticated quantitative techniques to solve research problems in these areas, giving our graduates a competitive advantage for careers in industry, government, or academia. 
 Applicants can either apply to single labs (direct entry), or apply to enter the rotation program, which gives students the opportunity to conduct research in three labs before being matched to a lab. Applications are due on December 1, 2026. Applicants should contact faculty and identify potential advisors before applying – you can begin by consulting the list of recruiting labs below.
 PhD Track in Translational Precision Medicine
In addition to our core program, applicants may also apply to a track in which each student focuses on a rare genetic disease. Developed with Cook Children's Medical Center, the track pairs laboratory research on disease mechanisms and models with exposure to specialty clinics, biotech and pharmaceutical partners, and patient advocacy organizations. This track prepares graduates to lead precision-medicine efforts in academia, industry, and advocacy. Fellowships are sponsored by partner foundations. Faculty accepting students in this track are indicated with asterisks*.
 Recruiting professors include:
Esther Betran (Ecology and Evolution; Genomics): The Betran Lab studies novelty in genomes: how new genes originate, what they do, and how they contribute to genome evolution, adaptation, and differences between species. Using Drosophila as a model, our current projects focus on duplicated genes and on genes and regulatory regions co-opted from transposable elements.
 Cara Boutte (Microbiology): The Boutte Lab studies how mycobacteria, including the pathogen Mycobacterium tuberculosis, build and alter their cell walls under different conditions. Because cell wall regulation under stress leads to antibiotic tolerance, our work helps explain how M. tuberculosis survives infection and antibiotic treatment.
 Todd Castoe* (Ecology and Evolution; Herpetology; Genomics): The Castoe Lab studies genome biology and evolutionary genomics: how genomes evolve and function, and how novel or extreme traits arise. We use snakes as models to investigate gene regulatory networks, regeneration, and speciation, and study schistosome parasites to address questions about disease transmission and human health. Our work integrates large-scale population and functional genomic datasets with computational approaches.
 Woo-Suk Chang* (Microbiology): The Chang Lab studies soil microbiomes in the context of climate change, working with farmers to implement climate-smart practices that reduce greenhouse gas emissions from soybean fields. The lab also studies probiotics and the human gut microbiome, including how fermented soybean products affect gut health and microbiome composition.
 Shashank Gandhi* (Genomics; Cell and Developmental Biology): The Gandhi Lab studies how stem cells interpret signals from their surroundings and, in turn, shape their environments to coordinate organ structure and function during embryonic development. We are particularly interested in the neural crest, a remarkable population of migratory stem cells that gives rise to diverse cell types and tissues, including components of the heart, the enteric nervous system, and craniofacial bone and cartilage. By combining genomics, advanced microscopy, and genome and epigenome engineering with chicken and mouse embryos and human stem cell-based models, we seek to uncover how cells communicate, make fate decisions, and work together to build functional organs. 
 Weiming Li* (Genomics; Bioinformatics; Cell and Developmental Biology): The Li Lab studies how extreme physiological stresses, such as cardiopulmonary bypass and cardiac arrest, reshape cell states, transcription, and the epigenome to drive inflammation and organ dysfunction. We integrate single-cell and spatial transcriptomics, epigenomics, computational biology, and mechanistic experiments in clinically relevant models and human samples, with the goal of improving survival and long-term neurological outcomes for children undergoing critical cardiovascular care.
 Daniela Palmer (Ecology and Evolution; Genomics): We are interested in understanding the genetic underpinnings of biodiversity, especially in sex-related traits. We study the evolution of sex chromosomes and other parts of the genome that contribute to sex-specific adaptation. Our research focuses on a group of insects known as treehoppers that show fascinating diversity in morphology, behavior, and beyond.
 Mark Pellegrino (Cell and Developmental Biology): The Pellegrino Lab studies how cells recover from mitochondrial stress through the mitochondrial unfolded protein response (UPRmt). We investigate the role of the UPRmt in aging, host-pathogen interactions and immunity, and coral stress resistance, using model systems including the nematode C. elegans, the jellyfish Cassiopea xamachana, and mice.
 Elena Perry (Ecology and Evolution; Genomics; Microbiology): The Perry Lab studies how bacterial genetic traits and interspecies interactions shape plant microbiome structure and function, combining microbial physiology, ecology, metabolomics, and high-throughput functional genomics. Our themes include how bacteria colonize plants, nutrient exchange within plant microbiomes, and how natural antibiotics produced by soil microbes affect native microbial communities and clinical antibiotic resistance.
 Anita Quintana* (Genomics; Cell and Developmental Biology): The Quintana lab seeks to understand the underlying mechanisms by which genetic (pathogenic) variants cause birth defects. We have a specific focus on birth defects that disrupt brain and craniofacial development, including how changes in cholesterol and vitamin B12 metabolism disrupt development and cause disease. Our laboratory uses zebrafish as a model system to study development. Zebrafish are an amazing developmental model because they are fertilized outside of their mother allowing for the visualization of development in real time.
 Qing Tang* (Microbiology): Bacterial physiology, pathogenesis, antimicrobial resistance, and host interactions of human pathogens including Listeria monocytogenes and Staphylococcus aureus. We investigate how bacteria respond to stress during antibiotic treatment and infection using biochemistry, microbiology, cell biology, genetics, and omics (spatial single-cell RNA-seq, bulk RNA-seq, proteomics), with both cell-culture and mouse models.
 Yoseop Yoon* (Genomics; Bioinformatics; Cell and Developmental Biology): The Yoon Lab studies biomolecular condensates, droplet-like structures in the cell nucleus that shape gene activity by organizing DNA and coordinating when and where RNA is processed. We ask how condensates form, how they regulate the biochemical reactions of RNA processing, and how changes in these structures may contribute to cancer.
 To apply, and for more information see:
https://www.uta.edu/academics/schools-colleges/science/departments/biology/graduate-programs/phd-program
 About UTA: 
UT Arlington is an R1-ranked research university, the second largest institution in the University of Texas system and one of the 10 fastest-growing public universities in the nation. We are a Hispanic-serving institution and rank #6 in the nation for ethnic diversity. 
 The Biology Department (http://www.uta.edu/biology) offers access to numerous resources including state-of-the-art labs, an Animal Care Facility, a Genomics Core Facility, the North Texas Genomics Center, the world-class Amphibian and Reptile Diversity Research Center, and the Shimadzu Institute for Research Technologies. These offer extensive and cutting-edge resources for high-throughput sequencing, imaging, proteomics, analytical chemistry, and more.
 About Arlington:
Arlington is situated in the Dallas-Fort Worth metroplex, affording access to numerous restaurants and entertainment opportunities (museums, zoos, aquariums, theatre, music, sports, microbreweries). The city of Arlington alone has 100 public parks, including River Legacy Parks, a 1,300-acre oasis on the Trinity River in the heart of north Arlington. Arlington is the home of the Dallas Cowboys’ stadium, the Texas Rangers’ ballpark, and Six Flags Over Texas. More information on the city of Arlington can be found at (www.arlington.org).
 Qualifications
Fundamental requirements include:
• Applicants must have completed their bachelor's degree in biology or a related field by summer 2027.
• Strong work ethic and independence
• Strong communication and teamwork skills
• Excellent English writing and speaking ability.
Contact
Ask Biology @ UTA
[email removed] (preferred contact method)

Description
Osprey Wilds Environmental Learning Center is a public, non-profit residential learning center on Grindstone Lake near Sandstone, MN that provides outdoor educational opportunities to diverse audiences in an intimate setting.

Residential and day-use environmental education  experiences for thousands of K-12 students from across the Midwest focus on a selection of adventure, team building, outdoor/environmental education, cultural, natural history and science, wildlife ecology, and renewable energy classes. We are accredited by Cognia, and have over 50 years of environmental education experience and an incredible variety of programs and audiences. 

Working at Osprey Wilds as a Fellow is a one-of-a-kind opportunity! Join our team and gain experience in current environmental education methods, as well as knowledge of Minnesota’s unique biomes and natural history through training seminars, direct mentorship, graduate level coursework, and on-the-job learning.

Key Responsibilities
Teach ecology, wildlife, adventure, and cultural classes to large and small groups of all ages, including evening and weekend programming.
Serve as the primary representative and host to visiting conference and retreat groups (includes being on-call for overnight visitors and serving food).
Plan and lead summer camp programming and free-time activities.
Attend weekly staff meetings and regular training throughout the year.
Provide basic husbandry for Osprey Wilds Animal Ambassadors, including raptors, corvids, mammals, invertebrates and herps.
Complete other self-directed projects or projects/tasks as assigned. 

Benefits
Compensation includes a $275/week stipend
Delicious, healthy meals during the week (when groups are present) made from locally sourced ingredients and produce from our Trapp Farm
Private room in staff housing adjacent to Grindstone Lake
Four days off per two-week pay period, 13 PTO days, accrual of up to 80 hours of paid sick leave
Access to an Employee Assistance Program
Employee discounts for events and lodging for family members and in the Osprey Wilds store

To Apply
Please send a resume, cover letter, and three references to Amy Heusinkvelt at [email removed].

402-285-2010

Description
Graduate student openings in organismal biology or physiological ecology at the University of Florida
  The Gillooly Lab in the Department of Biology at the University of Florida has openings for 1-2 graduate students beginning in Fall 2027. Research in the lab is diverse but generally falls under the category of comparative organismal biology or physiological ecology. Lab members use a variety of approaches, including mathematical modeling, experimentation and field studies. We share an interest in uncovering and explaining broad-scale patterns in organismal biology that can be used to better understand populations, communities and ecosystems in different environments.  Above all, we seek students that are creative, curious, and collaborative. Prospective students should contact Dr. Gillooly by email (gillooly “at” ufl.edu) to discuss possibilities. The deadline for application is December 1, 2026. More information regarding the program and the application is found here: https://biology.ufl.edu/graduate-programs/ , https://biology.ufl.edu/graduate-programs/application/

Description
The School of Fisheries, Aquaculture and Aquatic Sciences at Auburn University is seeking a highly qualified MS student to conduct research on recreational fishing at pay-lake operations starting in Spring 2027. The selected student will be responsible for completion of a research project related to economic valuation of recreational fishing, angler behavior, fish vulnerability to angling, and/or stocking optimization. The student will be responsible for planning, analysis, writing, sharing results via presentations and peer-reviewed publications, and completion of coursework. 
 Qualifications: B.S. in fisheries, economics, or closely related natural resource field with a minimum of a 3.0 GPA. Students with a strong work ethic, good verbal and written communication skills, and ability to work independently and as productive member of a research team are encouraged to apply. Previous research experience (from job, internship or undergraduate research) including surveys, writing, data management, and statistical analysis are a plus. 
 The graduate assistantship is for two years and consists of a 0.5 FTE (20 hours per week) commitment to working with the program. A tuition waiver is included in the assistantship. The expected start date is January 7, 2027.
 For more information about the School and our graduate programs please visit: Fisheries, Aquaculture and Aquatic Sciences | College of Agriculture
 To Apply: Please submit 1) a cover letter detailing your interest in the position and your qualifications, 2) curriculum vitae, 3) unofficial transcripts, 4) a list of three references and their contact information to Dr. Taryn Garlock ([email removed]). For full consideration, apply by November 8, 2026. Please direct any questions to Dr. Garlock ([email removed]). 
Contact
Taryn Garlock
[email removed] (preferred contact method)

Description
The Chattopadhyay Hydroecology Lab, led by Dr. Somsubhra Chattopadhyay at Texas State University, is recruiting a PhD student in environmental hydrology to start in August 2027. Funding is available for 4.5 years.

Texas rivers are changing fast: floods are getting flashier, droughts longer, and streams that once flowed year-round now go dry. The student will help work out what that means for the rivers and the life in them, combining ecohydrologic modelling and fieldwork in the Texas Hill Country. The project can grow in one of three directions:

Rivers on the edge of drying. When, where and why do Hill Country streams stop flowing, and what happens to connectivity and aquatic life when they do?
Forecasting rivers in a hotter, thirstier Texas. Use SWAT+ and data-driven models to project how climate, land use and water demand will reshape floods, low flows and environmental flows.
Linking flow to life. Pair hydrology with environmental DNA and field biodiversity data to find the flow conditions that keep rivers diverse and functioning.
The student will shape the final direction together with Dr. Chattopadhyay and will also lead one chapter that uses large-scale existing data or synthesizes existing research.

Applicants should have a background in hydrology, water resources engineering, environmental science, earth sciences, ecology or a related field. Experience with hydrologic modeling, GIS, R, Python or statistics is desirable. Strong quantitative skills and an interest in interdisciplinary research are especially welcome.

The student will be expected to mentor undergraduate researchers, be a collaborative member of the research group, and take part in Biology Department activities. The student will serve as a teaching assistant for 4 semesters. Applicants from all backgrounds are encouraged to apply, and international applicants are welcome. The degree is a PhD in Integrative and Applied Biology.

To apply: Complete the online application form by November 30, 2026: https://forms.gle/Pwr1TUGtZWYrvX5DA
The form asks for your CV, short answers about your interests and experience, and contact details for two references. Applications are accepted only through the form. Shortlisted applicants will be interviewed in December, and the selected candidate will then apply to the Texas State Graduate College by its February 1, 2027 deadline.

More about the lab: https://schatteco.github.io/chattopadhyayhydroecologylab/join.html

Description
The Borderlands Research Institute (BRI) at Sul Ross State University is seeking a motivated PhD or two Master’s students to conduct a project focused on movement ecology of cinnamon teal captured in southern Nevada on Pahranagat National Wildlife Refuge. This unique capture location lies in the heart of the interior Pacific Flyway and is a major bottleneck for birds moving through their annual cycle. This project will provide the opportunity to inform management decisions at multiple scales (i.e., local, regional, and national) by using (~ n = 100) GSM-GPS units that will address the objectives below. 

Objectives

1.      Investigate Migration Strategies using the generated GPS data to estimate time spent on Pahranagat National Wildlife Refuge allowing managers to time management decisions and estimate duck-use days needed to support Cinnamon teal and other key migratory gamebird species as they migrate through the area. Additionally, linkages between Pahranagat National Wildlife Refuge and associated breeding and wintering areas will inform conservation measures broadly. 
 2.      Perform Network Connectivity through a Random Forest modeling effort to investigate how important Pahranagat National Wildlife Refuge is to migratory game bird species such as Cinnamon teal as they are moving through managed wetland systems over the course of their annual cycle. 
Qualifications:

·         B.S. or M.S. in Wildlife Science, Natural Resources, Environmental Science, Ecology, or related field

·         Experience or coursework in GIS/remote sensing and quantitative analysis preferred

·         Demonstrated interest in movement ecology, wetland ecology, wetland dependent wildlife conservation, or resource selection

·         Strong written and verbal communication skills

·         Ability to work independently and collaboratively with agency partner

 Additional Information

Sul Ross State University is in the initial stages of establishing a PhD program on campus. As they work towards that accreditation an agreement has been established with Texas Tech University for the student to spend time on campus at both Universities for course work. Dr. Collins and Conway will be Co-PIs. The student will also work closely with biologists from Pahranagat NWR (Rob Vinson) and Pacific Flyway state agency biologists (e.g., Nevada Division of Wildlife, Utah Division of Wildlife, Arizona Game and Fish Department). The opportunity to be exposed to multiple agencies, Flyways, and a unique academic setting offers the student the ability to gain access to more resources and individuals than many of their peers.

ARS will deliver cutting-edge, scientific tools and innovative solutions for American farmers, producers, industry, and communities to support the nourishment and well-being of all people; sustain our nation’s agroecosystems and natural resources; and ensure the economic competitiveness and excellence of our agriculture. Research Project: Fusarium Head Blight is one of the most devastating diseases of wheat, barley, and other cereal crops and is a persistent threat to U.S. agriculture, causing economic losses exceeding $1B in epidemic years. This opportunity investigates how Fusarium causes disease by interacting with its hosts and how it produces harmful mycotoxins that accumulate in cereal grains during infection. Alongside your mentor, you will design experiments, collect and analyze data, and collaborate with lab members to achieve project goals. Description
Graduate Research Assistantship (M.S. or Ph.D.) – Aquatic Animal Health and Sustainable Aquaculture

Project:
Development of Integrated Disease Detection, Prevention, and Vaccine Strategies for Sustainable Aquaculture

Position Overview

The Aquatic One Health Lab in the Warnell School of Forestry and Natural Resources at the University of Georgia is seeking a highly motivated and self-disciplined graduate student to join our research program in aquatic animal health and sustainable aquaculture.

The successful applicant will contribute to research focused on aquatic disease diagnosis, pathogen detection, disease prevention, host-pathogen interactions, and vaccine development, with an emphasis on addressing emerging and existing health challenges in aquaculture.

The student will have the opportunity to develop an independent dissertation research program involving one or more of the following areas:

Development and application of molecular diagnostic tools for the detection of bacterial and viral pathogens in aquatic animals;
Isolation, characterization, and investigation of aquatic pathogens and infection dynamics;
Development and evaluation of vaccines for important bacterial and viral diseases of aquaculture species;
Investigation of fish immune responses to vaccination, infection, and immunostimulants;
Development and evaluation of disease prevention and management strategies for sustainable aquaculture;
Investigation of interactions among pathogens, host health, and environmental conditions.
The specific dissertation research project will be developed collaboratively based on the student's interests and background, as well as the laboratory's ongoing and emerging research programs.

The graduate student will become an active member of the Aquatic One Health Lab and will have opportunities to collaborate with faculty, graduate and undergraduate students, researchers, diagnostic laboratories, government agencies, aquaculture producers, and other industry partners. Depending on the assistantship arrangement, the student may also be expected to assist with teaching activities within the Warnell School.

Additional responsibilities will include designing and conducting experiments, analyzing and interpreting data, presenting research findings at scientific conferences and professional meetings, preparing manuscripts for publication in peer-reviewed journals, and contributing to a collaborative and supportive laboratory environment.

Qualifications

Required

B.S. or M.S. degree in aquaculture, fisheries, biology, microbiology, veterinary science, animal science, bioinformatics, or a related field;
Strong interest in microbiology, immunology, molecular biology, bioinformatics, aquatic animal health, or a related area;
Ability to work independently and collaboratively in a research environment;
Strong attention to detail and ability to follow and develop experimental protocols;
Strong written and oral communication skills;
Commitment to conducting rigorous, reproducible research and publishing findings in peer-reviewed journals. 
Salary and Benefits

The position will be supported through a combination of graduate research and teaching assistantships, with a competitive stipend, tuition support, and graduate student benefits, subject to University of Georgia and Warnell School policies and the availability of research funding.

Location

The student will be based in the Aquatic One Health Lab in the Warnell School of Forestry and Natural Resources at the University of Georgia in Athens, Georgia.

Research activities may also involve field work at aquaculture farms and hatcheries, diagnostic laboratories, and collaborating institutions.

Position Title: Ph.D. Graduate Assistantship – Optimizing Invasive Cattail Treatment Effectiveness for Native Vegetation, Waterfowl, and Marsh Birds in Prairie Wetlands

Location: Grand Forks, ND, with field work in western MN (Otter Tail, Pope, Stevens, Traverse, Big Stone, Swift, Chippewa, and Todd counties)

Start Date: Spring 2027 for fieldwork with the potential of a January or August 2027 official grad program start

Position Description: We are seeking a PhD student with broad interest in wetland habitat management and wetland biology/ecology (especially wetland plant, waterfowl, and marsh bird communities) to join a research team comparing the effectiveness and longevity of several treatments for invasive cattail in seasonal prairie pothole wetlands, with the goal of informing habitat management techniques for waterfowl and marsh birds. 

Invasive cattail species (Typha angustifolia, T. x glauca) have dramatically proliferated across North America’s prairie pothole region since the mid-twentieth century. Unlike native cattail, invasive cattail forms thick monocultures, impacting native plant diversity, displacing wildlife food plants, and disrupting habitat structure. The overarching research project is a before-after/control-impact study comparing the outcomes of four cattail treatment methods across approximately 50 wetlands in western Minnesota for the first 3 years following treatment. The selected candidate will collect and analyze post-treatment data, including (1) vegetation type and structure data from vegetation surveys and high-resolution aerial imagery from an uncrewed aerial system (UAS; i.e., a drone), (2) waterfowl and secretive marsh bird abundance from UAS surveys, and (3) waterfowl and secretive marsh bird occupancy from passive acoustic recording units. The selected candidate will analyze these data streams toward the goal of producing practical information for land managers to balance frequency of needed retreatment versus cost per treatment. The candidate will also participate in sharing results with natural resource managers and the public. Given the vast amount of data collected, there is the potential to develop additional questions of interest to the candidate.     

This research is highly collaborative, offering opportunity to engage with professionals in various career tracks and agencies/entities. Partners include scientists and wetland managers from the Minnesota Department of Natural Resources, the US Fish and Wildlife Service, Delta Waterfowl, and the University of Minnesota. Good communication skills will be key to success in this collaborative team.  

This research will have a heavy field travel component, with the PhD student stationed full-time in the field from April to August in 2027, 2028, and possibly 2029. During this time, the student will lead field technicians in data collection. Co-PIs will provide close support, including regular in-person presence. Field work will include piloting UAS’s, driving 4WD trucks and UTVs, hiking across prairie, and wading/collecting data in shallow wetlands with thick emergent vegetation, in a variety of weather conditions (cold early spring to hot summer temperatures).  

Minimum qualifications
·        Master’s degree in plant ecology, wildlife biology, biology, ecology, or a related field
·        Commitment to fostering an inclusive and respectful work environment
·        Strong communication and collaboration skills for working within a large research team
·        Interest in research spanning all project lines of inquiry (wetland management techniques, wetland plant biology/ecology, avian biology/ecology, wetland soils), and research experience pertinent to 1-2 of those topics
·        Willingness to work full-time in the field April-August (with field lodging provided by University of North Dakota)
·        Field work experience relevant to at least one of the project data collection methods
·        Already possess or willing to obtain (with guidance from PIs) a FAA Part 107 license (Remote Pilot Certificate) for operating UAS
·        Experience with statistical analysis of biological data and analysis software (e.g., R)
·        Experience with GIS software (e.g., ArcGIS) 
·        Strong writing skills
·        Experience prioritizing research project tasks and setting realistic timelines for completion

Preferred qualifications
·        Experience leading field crews in data collection
·        At least one peer-reviewed scientific publication
·        Research experience in multiple lines of project inquiry (wetland management techniques, wetland plant biology/ecology, avian biology/ecology, wetland soils) 
·        Field work experience with multiple project data collection methods (e.g., waterfowl surveys using UAS with thermal and EO sensors, plant surveys, passive acoustic recording units, creating orthomosaics from UAS imagery, wetland soil sampling) 

Salary and benefits: $30,240/year plus a tuition waiver. Student is expected to cover the modest student fees that are not an expense that can be covered by grants. The position is primarily funded through a research assistantship through June 2030. The selected candidate will be expected to work a teaching assistantship for 1-2 semesters to develop teaching/mentoring experience and to meet project budget constraints.

For full consideration, please apply by November 15, 2026. Questions about the position may be addressed to Dr. Ellis-Felege ([email removed]) and/or Dr. Megan Fitzpatrick ([email removed])

Position Description
Drs. Tyler Steven Coleman and Kyle R. Piller are recruiting two highly motivated M.S. students to begin in Spring 2027 in the Department of Biological Sciences and Center for Environmental Research at Southeastern Louisiana University. Both positions are supported by a funded, interdisciplinary research project investigating blue crab (Callinectes sapidus) ecology, movement, population connectivity, and environmental health throughout the beautiful and unique Lake Pontchartrain Basin in coastal Louisiana. Each assistantship includes a 12-month stipend of $18,000 per year for two years and a full tuition waiver, with research support and opportunities for professional conference travel.

Location
The student will be housed in the Center for Environmental Research and the Department of Biological Sciences at Southeastern Louisiana University in Hammond, Louisiana.
 Project
The two students will pursue complementary research objectives while working closely on field sampling, data collection, and interdisciplinary research activities.
Position 1: Movement Ecology and Population Dynamics (Dr. Tyler Steven Coleman)
The selected student will lead a large-scale blue crab mark–recapture study to investigate movement patterns and population dynamics throughout the Lake Pontchartrain Basin. This position involves extensive boat-based fieldwork, overnight travel, data management, and quantitative analyses.
Position 2: Population Genetics and Molecular Ecology (Dr. Kyle R. Piller)
The selected student will investigate blue crab population genetic structure and connectivity using molecular approaches. Research will involve genetic sampling, laboratory analyses, and bioinformatics to interpret molecular data and better understand population connectivity across the basin.
Both students will have opportunities to incorporate environmental chemistry, contaminant exposure, and histological analyses into their thesis research, depending on their interests. Students will receive training in research design, data analysis, and scientific communication, with opportunities to present findings at scientific conferences and publish in peer-reviewed journals.
 Qualifications
Applicants must have a B.S. degree in biology, fisheries, marine biology, ecology, wildlife, or a related discipline; strong communication and organizational skills; and the ability to work independently and collaboratively.
Preference will be given to applicants with relevant field or laboratory research experience. Both positions involve fieldwork throughout coastal Louisiana, including long days outdoors in variable weather conditions and occasional overnight travel. A valid driver’s license is required.

Research Activities
·      Designing and conducting a large-scale mark–recapture study.
·      Extensive field sampling from boats throughout the Lake Pontchartrain Basin and adjacent coastal waters.
·      Quantifying blue crab movement patterns and population dynamics.
·      Managing, synthesizing, and analyzing ecological datasets.
·      Collaborating with researchers conducting environmental chemistry, histology, and molecular analyses.
·      Applying quantitative approaches to fisheries data.
·      Presenting research findings at regional or national scientific meetings.
·      Publishing results in peer-reviewed journals. 
Students interested in fisheries ecology, marine and estuarine ecology, movement ecology, quantitative ecology, or applied natural resource management are especially encouraged to apply.

1.    Cover letter describing research interests, relevant experience, career goals, and the position(s) of interest.
2.    Curriculum vitae or résumé.
3.    Unofficial transcripts.

Applications should be emailed to both Dr. Coleman ([email removed]) and Dr. Piller ([email removed]). Applicants interested in both positions are encouraged to indicate this in their cover letters. If you have any questions, please contact either Dr. Coleman or Dr. Piller.
 Applications will be reviewed immediately and will continue until both positions are filled. Selected applicants will be invited to participate in virtual interviews. Because of the anticipated January 2027 start date, interested applicants are strongly encouraged to apply as soon as possible.

 Position Title: Ph.D. Graduate Assistantship – Population Dynamics of North Pacific Albatrosses

Position Description: We are seeking a highly motivated Ph.D. student to pursue research that bridges seabird ecology, demographic modeling, and wildlife conservation. The successful candidate will leverage extensive long-term datasets to understand the intrinsic and extrinsic factors driving populations of two species of North Pacific albatrosses – Laysan Albatross (Mōlī) and Black-footed Albatross (Ka‘upu). The research will primarily focus on breeding colonies at Midway Atoll, with potential expansion to include populations on other islands. This project has a strong quantitative focus. The core of the research involves the development of advanced demographic models, including Integrated Population Models, to understand how local and broad-scale environmental factors and fisheries affect population status, vital rates, and demographic trends. However, the student will have significant latitude to co-develop specific research questions and analytical approaches. The student may have the opportunity (contingent upon availability of funds) to participate in field deployments to the Pacific to assist with ongoing monitoring efforts and collect targeted field data in support of their specific project objectives. The successful applicant will be expected to publish their research in peer-reviewed scientific journals and present their findings at scientific conferences. This is a highly collaborative initiative, and the student will work closely with a diverse team of researchers, field biologists, and wildlife managers, including partners at the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS) and the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS). The successful candidate will pursue a Ph.D. degree in Wildlife and Rangeland Sciences with the Caesar Kleberg Wildlife Research Institute and Department of Rangeland and Wildlife Sciences, Texas A&M University-Kingsville. 

Required Qualifications: 
M.S. in Wildlife Science, Ecology, Statistics, or closely related field from an accredited university.
Strong quantitative and problem-solving skills, with experience in ecological modeling and statistical computing.
Excellent written and verbal communication skills, including the ability to engage with diverse audiences (scientists, wildlife managers, and the public).
Strong work ethic with the ability to work both independently and collaboratively within a research team.

Preferred Qualifications:
Demonstrated record of applied ecological research through peer-reviewed publications, presentations, or other scholarly activities.
Experience with demographic modeling within Bayesian frameworks (e.g., JAGS, Nimble).
Experience with geospatial technologies (e.g., GIS) and remote sensing data products (e.g., climate and oceanographic data).
Knowledge of seabird ecology or avian population dynamics
Experience conducting basic field ecology.

Stipend/Salary: $2,500/month plus benefits (medical package available after completion of waiting period). Nonresident tuition is waived (resident tuition and fees apply). Assistance of resident-tuition fees will be provided up to but not exceeding $12,000/year.
 
Start Date: January 2027.

Application Deadline: We will begin reviewing applications beginning 7 October 2026 and will continue until a suitable candidate is selected.

To Apply: Application packet must consist of: (1) cover letter summarizing your experience and interest in the position; (2) CV; (3) unofficial academic transcripts; (4) contact information for two professional references; and (5) one writing sample.  Please send application materials (as a single PDF file) or address any questions regarding the position to Dr. Chris Malachowski ([email removed]; Caesar Kleberg Wildlife Research Institute, Texas A&M University-Kingsville) using the email subject line of ‘Albatross Demography Assistantship’.
 
Texas law requires that males 18 through 25 show proof of compliance with Federal Selective Service law in order to be eligible for employment. Selected candidate must pass a pre-employment background investigation to be hired for this position. EEO/AA/ADA

 Senior Research Scientist and Associate Director for Research –Savannah River Ecology Laboratory 
 The University of Georgia’s Savannah River Ecology invites applications for a fiscal-year (12-month) position as a Senior Research Scientist with a primarily administrative appointment as an Associate Director for Research.  The successful applicant will be located at the Savannah River Ecology Laboratory in Aiken, S.C. and will report to the Director of the Savannah River Ecology Laboratory. This position will be 0.85 EFT in administration, 0.10 EFT in research, and 0.05 EFT service. 

Administrative Responsibilities:  The successful candidate will serve as Associate Director for Research for the Savannah River Ecology Laboratory and will support the SREL Director in a variety of administrative duties, including:  Development of external funding opportunities for faculty and staff, strategic planning for development of facilities and equipment to support ongoing and new research initiatives at SREL, supervision and evaluation of research professionals, support staff, and other positions related to supporting the research mission of SREL, development and updating of policies and procedures governing SREL’s compliance with DOE, UGA, and other applicable regulatory entities related to SREL’s research mission, assisting with the compilation and writing of annual reports to DOE, UGA, or other applicable entities, budget development, and other duties as assigned. 

Research Responsibilities:  The successful candidate is expected to serve as an adjunct professor and member of the graduate faculty in an appropriate department or school at UGA and will be involved in graduate education via co-advising of graduate students and service on graduate student committees.  Professional service to groups such as state and federal agencies, non-governmental organizations, professional societies, and the public also is expected as is significant interaction with colleagues and students in other disciplines represented at SREL, UGA, and the broader academic community. 

Qualifications:  Applicants must have a PhD in an appropriate field (biological, ecological, or environmental sciences), with a record of sustained research productivity and evidence of excellence in research administration commensurate with time since degree.  The candidate must have a minimum of 10 years of demonstrated administrative experience with personnel, budgets, facilities and funding development.  The candidate should have the ability to interact with colleagues from a diversity of disciplines on the planning, logistics, infrastructure, and implementation of research programs conducted by the Savannah River Ecology Laboratory faculty.  Preference will be given to candidates who have an administrative background within or in close interface with federal research programs, including the development and administration of multi-year Cooperative Agreements with federal partners.  

Savannah River Ecology Laboratory: The successful candidate will be located at the Savannah River Ecology Laboratory in Aiken, SC.  The Savannah River Ecology Laboratory is a research unit of the University of Georgia located on the 300 mi2 Savannah River Site, a Department of Energy facility near Aiken, SC. With a staff of over 200 faculty members, postdocs, research professionals, technicians, and graduate students, the laboratory pursues basic and applied research at multiple levels of ecological organization, from atoms to ecosystems. SREL also provides opportunities for graduate and undergraduate research training, and service to the community through environmental outreach. Throughout its 75+ year history SREL has strived to acquire and communicate knowledge that contributes to sound ecological stewardship.

Compensation:
$30,000 per year for 2.5 years for MS
Positions include tuition waiver and eligibility for university health benefits package
Summer field housing provided

Start date:  Flexible (January-May 2027) 

Application deadline:  November 15, 2026 (or until filled) 
 Responsibilities:  I am seeking a MS student to help assess the status and guide recovery of the federally endangered Spruce Fir Moss Spider (SFMS) and its microhabitat in high elevation spruce-fir ecosystems of the southern Appalachians. Specifically, the student will leverage existing data to estimate the probability of SFMS occupancy across potentially suitable habitat units, use environmental logger data to investigate how spider microhabitats were impacted by Hurricane Helene, and design/implement surveys to assess and guide habitat restoration and recovery efforts in spruce-fir ecosystems. Responsibilities will include analyzing spider survey data collected under a long-term monitoring protocol, assisting with spider surveys in high elevation forests, deploying and maintaining environmental sensors/loggers, conducting geospatial and statistical analyses, developing databases, writing a MS proposal, thesis, and technical reports, and completing coursework pursuant to a MS degree. The selected candidate will be advised by Dr. Cathy Jachowski and will work with a wide range of collaborators from state and federal agencies, NGOs, and universities. 
  Project Description: Hurricane Helene caused widespread flooding, landslides, and destruction across the southern Appalachian region in September 2024. These impacts caused long-term and potentially permanent changes to terrestrial and aquatic habitat distribution, ecosystem structure, and function. Field evaluations and monitoring are required to understand how baseline ecological conditions changed following these large-scale, geological changes in terrestrial and aquatic habitats. Graduate students working on this project will be part of a dynamic and multi-disciplinary team at Clemson University with expertise across the fields of forestry, wildlife, fisheries, and fire ecology. Team members will work closely with federal, state, and non-governmental organizations to communicate findings and inform ongoing, on-the-ground restoration and recovery efforts aimed at focal species, ecosystems and important forest resources.   
  Candidates must possess: 
·      A bachelor’s degree in wildlife, fisheries, ecology, biology, natural resources, or an equivalent field 
·      Competitive practical experience assisting with wildlife or ecological research 
·      An enthusiasm and interest in developing strong quantitative skills 
·      Ability to backpack 10+ miles over rugged terrain and work in remote settings 
·      Willingness to travel for extended periods during the summer; Field housing will be provided, but occasional backpack camping is required 
·      Demonstrated excellence in verbal, written, and quantitative skills 
·      A valid US driver’s license 
   Ideal candidates will possess some combination of the following: 
·         Working knowledge of the Southern Appalachian Spruce-Fir ecosystem 
·         Arthropod/spider survey experience and identification skills 
·         Bryophyte/lichen identification skills 
·         Technical writing experience (peer reviewed journals and scientific reports) 
·         Proficiency in database management software (Microsoft Excel and Access) 
·         Experience with digital map and data collection tools (ArcGIS, Survey123, FieldMaps, Avenza Maps) 
·         Experience communicating with state and federal agencies and NGOs 
·         Training, supervising, and coordinating field crews 

To apply, please email your application to Dr. Cathy Jachowski ([email removed]) with a subject line of “MS Application: SFMS”. To ensure full consideration, compile the components listed below into a single PDF file: 
1) Cover letter describing your interest in the project and career goals 
2) Current Resume/CV, including 3 academic or professional references 
3) Unofficial undergraduate transcripts 
The GRE is not required for admission to Clemson or to work with our team, but applicants may include GRE scores if they think it will improve the attractiveness of their application.

Description
 Assistant Research Scientist in Herpetology –Savannah River Ecology Laboratory 
 The University of Georgia’s Savannah River Ecology (SREL) invites applications for an Academic-Year (9-month) position as an Assistant Research Scientist.  The successful applicant will be located at the Savannah River Ecology Laboratory in Aiken, S.C. and will report to the Director of the Savannah River Ecology Laboratory. This position will be 0.11 EFT in Instruction, 0.67 EFT in research, 0.11 EFT in Service, and 0.11 EFT in Program Administration.  Funding for this position will be provided by SREL, which is supported in part through a cooperative agreement with the Department of Energy, and the University of Georgia Research Institute, a research unit focused on enhancing UGA’s relationships with federal mission driven agencies. 

Responsibilities: The successful candidate is expected to develop an extramurally funded and internationally recognized research program focused in herpetology, with focal disciplinary expertise in ecophysiology, ecotoxicology, risk assessment, and conservation. The successful candidate will be expected to serve as an adjunct professor and member of the graduate faculty in an applicable department or school at UGA and will be involved in graduate instruction via advising of graduate students and service on graduate student committees. Professional service to groups such as state and federal agencies, non-governmental organizations, professional societies, and the public also is expected, as is significant interaction with colleagues and students in other disciplines represented at SREL, UGA, and the broader academic community. The successful candidate also will be expected to maintain a research program that complies with all applicable regulatory and reporting requirements pertinent to the Savannah River Site, state, and federal regulations.  

Qualifications: Applicants must have a PhD in an appropriate field (Biology, Wildlife Ecology, Ecology, or related field), with demonstrated potential for research. The candidate should have a strong background in herpetology and species conservation, as well as demonstrated expertise in ecophysiology and ecotoxicology and a broad understanding of risk assessment as related to the biotic fate and transport of contaminants in the environment. The candidate should have the ability to interact with colleagues from a diversity of disciplines on the development of research proposals related to the conservation of reptile species as well as to the quantification of the physiological and toxicological risks of contaminant exposure in reptiles. Preference will be given to candidates having a record of excellence in research and service commensurate with time since degree, and postdoctoral experience is highly desired. Past funding success with federal mission agencies such as SERDP and DOE is preferred.  Applicants with expertise in ecophysiology, ecotoxicology, and risk assessment in turtles and snakes are especially encouraged to apply. 

Savannah River Ecology Laboratory: The successful candidate will be located at the Savannah River Ecology Laboratory in Aiken, SC.  The Savannah River Ecology Laboratory is a research unit of the University of Georgia located on the 300 mi2 Savannah River Site, a Department of Energy facility near Aiken, SC. With a staff of over 200 faculty members, postdocs, research professionals, technicians, and graduate students, the laboratory pursues basic and applied research at multiple levels of ecological organization, from atoms to ecosystems. SREL also provides opportunities for graduate and undergraduate research training, and service to the community through environmental outreach. Throughout its 75+ year history SREL has strived to acquire and communicate knowledge that contributes to sound ecological stewardship. 

Application: To ensure full consideration, candidates must submit a cover letter, curriculum vitae, statement of research interests, unofficial transcripts of all college-level work, copies of up to three recent relevant publications, and contact information for three references. Review of complete applications will begin on December 1, 2026 and continue until the position is filled. Individuals considered for potential interviews will be required to submit official college transcripts and three reference letters. University policy requires all candidates to consent to a background investigation (www.hr.uga.edu). Finalists will be required to provide a signed consent form authorizing the University to conduct a background check. The background investigation will be conducted on a post offer/pre-employment basis. The starting date is negotiable but a spring 2027 start date is desired. All applicants MUST apply online at  ugajobsearch.com/postings/search (posting number F2856P). No paper applications will be accepted. For further questions, please contact Dr. Xiaoyu Xu, Chair, Assistant Research Scientist in Herpetology Search Committee, Savannah River Ecology Laboratory, Drawer E, Aiken, SC 29802, [email removed] 

The University of Georgia is an Equal Opportunity/Affirmative Action employer. All qualified applicants will receive consideration for employment without regard to race, color, religion, sex, national origin, ethnicity, age, genetic information, disability, gender identity, sexual orientation, or protected veteran status. Persons needing accommodations or assistance with the accessibility of materials related to this search are encouraged to contact Central HR ([email removed]). 

Contact
Xiaoyu Xu

Description

ARS Office/Lab and Location: A research opportunity is currently available with the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA), Agricultural Research Service (ARS), located in Mayaguez, Puerto Rico.

The Agricultural Research Service (ARS) is the U.S. Department of Agriculture's chief scientific in-house research agency with a mission to find solutions to agricultural problems that affect Americans every day from field to table. ARS will deliver cutting-edge, scientific tools and innovative solutions for American farmers, producers, industry, and communities to support the nourishment and well-being of all people; sustain our nation’s agroecosystems and natural resources; and ensure the economic competitiveness and excellence of our agriculture. The vision of the agency is to provide global leadership in agricultural discoveries through scientific excellence.

Research Project: This project aims to evaluate the susceptibility of different coffee varieties to coffee leaf rust (CLR) and to assess the potential of natural biocontrol agents (mycoparasites) against Hemileia vastatrix. You will gain experience preparing fungal growth media and using standard laboratory equipment such as autoclaves, sterilizers, centrifuges, and homogenizers. You will also learn to identify key symptoms and signs of CLR, and conduct disease surveys (assessing incidence and severity) across coffee fields in Puerto Rico.

Learning Objectives: Under the guidance of a mentor, you will:

Learn to evaluate coffee-variety susceptibility to coffee leaf rust (CLR) caused by Hemileia vastatrix.
Gain experience assessing natural fungal biocontrol agents, including mycoparasites, for their potential to suppress CLR.
Develop laboratory skills in preparing fungal media and operating standard equipment such as autoclaves, sterilizers, centrifuges, and homogenizers.
Learn to recognize CLR symptoms and signs and conduct field disease surveys measuring disease incidence and severity in Puerto Rican coffee farms.
Prepare H. vastatrix inoculum and conduct pathogenicity assays using spore suspensions on coffee plants and detached leaf tissues.
Build molecular-biology skills through DNA extraction, PCR amplification, and sequence analysis of CLR pathogens and associated mycoparasites.
Gain practical greenhouse and field-management experience, including coffee planting, fertilization, weed management, irrigation, and pesticide application under established protocols.
Strengthen experimental-design, plant-pathology, data-collection, and disease-management skills relevant to sustainable coffee production.
Through these activities, you will develop or strengthen practical skills in plant pathology, disease evaluation, and plant-pathogen interactions.

Mentor(s): The mentor for this opportunity is Luz Serrato-Diaz ([email removed]). If you have questions about the nature of the research, please contact the mentor(s).

Anticipated Appointment Start Date: January 2027. Start date is flexible and will depend on a variety of factors.

Appointment Length: The appointment will initially be for six months but may be renewed upon recommendation of ARS and is contingent on the availability of funds.

Level of Participation: The appointment is full time.

Citizenship Requirements: This opportunity is available to U.S. citizens only.

ORISE Information: This program, administered by ORAU through its contract with the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) to manage the Oak Ridge Institute for Science and Education (ORISE), was established through an interagency agreement between DOE and ARS. Participants do not become employees of USDA, ARS, DOE or the program administrator, and there are no employment-related benefits. Proof of health insurance is required for participation in this program. Health insurance can be obtained through ORISE.

Questions: Please visit our Program Website. After reading, if you have additional questions about the application process, please email [email removed] and include the reference code for this opportunity.

Qualifications
The qualified candidate should be currently pursuing or have received a bachelor’s or master’s degree in the one of the relevant fields. Degree must have been received within the past one year or anticipated to be received by 6/30/2027.

Preference is placed on applicants with a bachelor's degree or applicants who are currently pursuing a master's degree.

Knowledge of plant biology, microbiology, plant pathology.
A degree of independence and critical thinking.

About Audubon
The National Audubon Society is a leading nonprofit conservation organization with 120 years of science-based, community-driven impact, dedicated to protecting birds and the places they need, today and tomorrow. Birds are powerful indicators of our planet’s health, acting as sentinels that warn us of environmental change and inspire action. Audubon works across the Western Hemisphere, driven by the understanding that what is good for birds is good for the planet. Through a collaborative, bipartisan approach across habitats, borders, and the political spectrum, Audubon drives meaningful and lasting conservation outcomes. With 800 staff and over 1.9 million supporters, Audubon is a dynamic and ever-growing force committed to ensuring a better planet for both birds and people for generations to come. Learn more at www.audubon.org and on Facebook, Twitter and Instagram @audubonsociety.

Position Summary:
Audubon California is seeking two fellows for a program dedicated to engaging a broad diversity of communities to create meaningful conservation solutions that work for birds, nature, and people. The Community Conservation Fellowship seeks to build lasting relationships between local communities and Audubon. Working at the Richardson Bay Audubon Center & Sanctuary in the San Francisco Bay Area, the Fellows will engage communities in nature, environmental advocacy, and climate resilience over a nine month period beginning January 2026.
 With mentorship from Audubon staff, the Fellows will contribute to conservation and outreach work at the Richardson Bay Audubon Center and through the San Francisco Bay Program.  Throughout the fellowship, fellows will receive training and gain the skills necessary for hands-on habitat restoration, leadership development, community stewardship, and advocacy training. Through center-based programming, Fellows will practice and develop skills by working with youth and communities – building up student leaders, advocates, and land stewards. Fellows will co-design with Audubon staff a series of outdoor community events and projects that target diverse, multi-generational audiences. Additionally, the Fellow will work with the San Francisco Bay Program Manager during restoration field workdays.  Through hands on learning, the Fellows will learn various surveying and monitoring techniques at various field sites.
 This job requires a culturally competent, organized, and responsible person who is an excellent communicator that can work effectively as part of a team and independently. The successful applicant must have an enthusiasm for the outdoors, and a willingness to learn, teach, and share actively with community groups.

Fellows should be a resident of the SF Bay Area or agree to on-site housing at the Richardson Bay Audubon Center & Sanctuary.

This role is on-site at the Richardson Bay Audubon Center and Sanctuary.

Maintains and fosters culture of safety.

Description
Florida Grasshopper Sparrow Internship 

 

Interns receive housing and a monthly stipend of $2,400 (before taxes) 

Summer Term: March 10th 2027-September 11th 2027 (Move in date: March 10th) 

 Apply Now: https://www.volgistics.com/appform/594518419  

 

Passionate about Passerines? Join our team! 

The Florida grasshopper sparrow (Ammodramus savannarum floridanus) is one of the most endangered birds in North America. Since 2019, White Oak has bred and released over 1,000 sparrows. White Oak’s minimal handling management model has led to sparrows that survive post-release and thrive, continuing future generations in the wild. This recovery program has robust partnerships with organizations including the US Fish and Wildlife Service and the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission.  

Interns experience this conservation program first-hand, working side-by-side with staff at White Oak. Focusing on ex situ animal care, interns work with sparrows through breeding seasons and winters, maintaining habitats, completing daily care needs and conducting observations. While interns see field team members and wildlife biologists during their internship, interns are not guaranteed the opportunity to observe the in-situ aspects of the program that are managed by partner organizations.  

The Florida Grasshopper Sparrow Conservation Internship requires a high degree of flexibility and a commitment to the assigned schedule and duties of the program. We are proud to have graduates who now work in field crews, zoological facilities, or who have pursued higher education in graduate programs focused on conservation. 

 

Career-Ready Skills & Learning Opportunities  

Interns are provided with a variety of technical skills and knowledge that makes them excellent candidates for roles in conservation facilities such as:  

Diet preparation, insect management, feeding, and cleaning  
Bird introductions and management  
Observation skills and knowledge of sparrow behavior, including identifying vocalizations and tracking individual birds by colored band  
Safe avian capture, hand restraint, and transportation  
Habitat maintenance including landscaping and fabrication  
Research skills including sample collection, camera trapping, video monitoring, rigorous daily data management, and reporting  
General reintroduction techniques including pre-release conditioning  
Artificial incubation and hatching (Summer only)  
Egg management and candling (Summer only)  
Hand-rearing passerines as needed (Summer only)  
Non-chemical fire ant control methods (Winter only) Prescribed fire techniques and participation (Winter only) 
 

Eligibility Requirements 

Applicants must meet all requirements and submit an online application including all required materials to be considered. 

Preference for recent college graduates or early career professionals  
Previous avian experience required, passerine handling and mist-netting experience preferred  
Keen eyesight to identify small birds and bands from a distance  
Good hearing ability to differentiate soft/quiet sounds and calls  
Hold a valid driver’s license and health insurance  
Able to pass a drug test upon starting  
Legally able to work in the United States (US Citizen, Permanent Resident, or hold an Employment Authorization Document)  
Able to work well independently and in a team environment  
Able to work evenings, weekends and holidays  
Experienced and comfortable working outside in high heat and humidity  
Strong attention to detail and data management skills  
High drive to learn, take on challenges, and stay motivated  
Be flexible to changing environments, priorities, or animal care needs  
Able to lift 50 lbs. repetitively, and remain standing, walking or crouched over for long periods of time  
Able to work 40 hours per week for the duration of the internship 
 

Living at White Oak 

Interns receive on-site housing during the internship. Housing is not available for spouses/partners/dependents or pets. Furniture, linens, towels and kitchen supplies including cookware, flatware, and dishes are provided. Interns will be assigned weekly chores and may be assigned a roommate of the same gender. 

 

Required Application Materials 

Interested applicants must fill out an online application. Questions? Email [email removed]

Description
Our research internship program is designed for undergraduate and graduate students, as well as recent graduates who want to gain practical field experience in tropical ecology and conservation or need to complete an internship as part of their university studies. Based at Cloudbridge Nature Reserve in the Talamanca Mountains of Costa Rica, interns contribute directly to our ongoing conservation and research efforts while developing the skills needed to plan, conduct, analyze, and communicate scientific research.

Develop your own research project

The main component of the internship is developing and conducting a short-term research study that benefits the reserve while aligning with your interests and, where applicable, your university's academic requirements. Research topics are developed in consultation with our Science team. Before arriving, interns must submit a research proposal for approval, and a video call will be arranged to discuss the project and ensure it is feasible within the available time and resources.

Research internships require a minimum commitment of 11 weeks. This allows sufficient time to collect data, analyze results, and write up your research before leaving the reserve. All interns are expected to present their findings at the midpoint and at the end of their stay, and submit a written report before departure.

Fieldwork and daily responsibilities

Research at Cloudbridge is a hands-on experience in a challenging natural environment. Projects can be physically demanding, often requiring hiking five days a week through steep terrain and working in variable, sometimes rainy, weather conditions.

Interns must be self-motivated, manage their own work schedules, follow research protocols carefully, complete tasks on time, maintain accurate records, and enter collected data into the appropriate databases. Our Science team provides guidance, but interns are expected to take responsibility for their projects and seek help when needed.

In addition to their research, interns contribute to the daily running of the reserve. Responsibilities include communal cleaning, taking turns welcoming hikers at the Welcome Centre alongside other interns and volunteers, and participating in reserve and community activities, such as monthly recycling sorting. The program also includes weekly birdwatching, occasional night walks, and presentations by interns and visiting researchers, offering further opportunities to learn about the reserve's biodiversity and ongoing scientific work.

Duration and costs

The minimum duration for a research internship is 11 weeks. Accommodation and project fees depend on the length of your stay:

$28 USD per day for stays of 11 weeks to less than 12 weeks.

$22 USD per day for stays of 12 weeks or longer.

These rates include a dormitory room, Wi-Fi, hot showers, shared bathrooms, and access to a shared kitchen.

Food and cooking are the responsibility of each intern. Most participants spend approximately $8–$10 USD per day on groceries for a basic, mostly vegetarian diet.

Cloudbridge staff organize a weekly order from a local farmers' market. Interns can select the produce they need from a list, and staff will collect the order the following day. Payment for this service is cash-only, so please bring sufficient cash to cover your purchases throughout your stay.

A $200 USD deposit is required to confirm your place in the program. This amount is credited toward your accommodation fees for the final two weeks of your agreed stay. If you leave more than two weeks before your agreed departure date, the deposit is normally forfeited, although exceptional circumstances will be considered.

How to apply

To apply, email [email removed] with the following information:

Your CV or résumé, including your academic background and relevant experience.

Contact details for two references who can comment on your suitability for the internship.

Your preferred arrival and departure dates. Please note that internship start dates must fall on a Sunday, and the minimum stay is 11 weeks.

A short statement of motivation explaining why you would like to join our program.

Research interests or project ideas, if you already have a particular topic in mind. You do not need to have a fully developed research proposal at this stage.

Once we receive your application, we will contact your references. If their feedback is positive, we will proceed with your acceptance into the program. You will then work with our Science team to identify a suitable research topic and develop a proposal for approval. We will also confirm your internship dates and arrange a video call to discuss your project. 

An internship at Cloudbridge is an opportunity to contribute to real conservation work, develop independent research skills, and experience the complexity and beauty of a tropical cloud forest. We welcome motivated students and graduates who are ready to take an active role in research and the daily life of the reserve.

Contact
Blanca Cejalvo Insausti

Detailed Position Information
The Department of Geography & the Environment at the University of Alabama (https://geography.ua.edu/) seeks an assistant professor (9-month, tenure track) broadly trained in Environmental Science, Earth Science, or Physical Geography. The successful candidate will be expected to teach Introduction to Environmental Science (a large enrollment, natural lab science credit course) and develop courses in atmospheric, landscape, forest, and/or river systems designed to engage undergraduates in our Environmental Science and Geography degree programs through experiential-based learning. A Ph.D. in Environmental Science, Earth Science, Physical Geography, or a closely related field is required at the time of appointment.

Potential areas of expertise may include landscape ecology, soil, biogeography, geomorphology, conservation, biodiversity, natural resources, environmental pollution, climatology, water resources, and/or physical hydrology. While the position is open to a wide range of specialties, some integration of human-environmental interactions is preferred. Successful candidates will be expected to develop an externally funded research program that is nationally and internationally regarded within their area of expertise, while delivering high-quality, engaged teaching. 

About the Department of Geography & the Environment (GYE): Through the efforts of 28 total faculty members, the GYE Department offers undergraduate degrees in Environmental Science (BS), Geography (BA/BS), and graduate degrees in Geography (MS and PhD). Currently, there are ~200 undergraduate majors, and ~60 graduate students. Ranked in the top 15 Geography programs for research production by Academic Analytics, faculty research centers on three areas: Earth Systems and Environmental Science, Environment and Society, and Geographic Information Systems and Remote Sensing. The GYE Department is housed in two buildings (Bevill Energy Building and the Shelby Interdisciplinary Sciences Building), and these spaces include several wet labs and computational labs, as well as newly renovated offices and meeting spaces.

The Department of Geography and the Environment sits within the Barefield College of Arts & Sciences (BCAS). Eighty percent of the University of Alabama’s core curriculum is offered through BCAS. The College also houses several educational and research resources, including the Alabama Museum of Natural History and Moundville Archeological Park, the University of Alabama’s Arboretum, the J. Nicholene Bishop Biological Station, and the Center for Freshwater Studies, which offers aquatic chemistry services. BCAS supports faculty professional development through sabbaticals and pre-tenure leaves, as well.

UA is home to the Alabama Water Institute (AWI), which serves as a hub of water-focused research and education, for federal agencies co-located on the UA campus, including the NOAA National Water Center and the U.S. Geological Survey’s Hydrologic Instrumentation Facility, as well as being the home of the Cooperative Institute for Research to Operations in Hydrology (CIROH), the Global Water Security Center, and CONSERVE. Numerous members of the Department of Geography and the Environment are affiliates of the Alabama Water Institute and conduct CIROH-funded research in continental to watershed scale hydrologic modeling, non-contact water observation, geospatial analyses, and social dimensions of water hazards. Three of the AWI’s key educational programs, the Water Prediction Innovators Summer Institute, the USGS FLOW Academy, and the NSF-funded National Science Traineeship Program: Water R2O are led by faculty in the Department of Geography and the Environment. In addition to providing exceptional professional training for our students, these programs offer graduate student and postdoctoral fellow recruitment opportunities for faculty at UA.

The state of Alabama is one of the most biologically and geomorphologically diverse landscapes in North America, and it is crossed by 17 major river basins. This makes the state an incredible living laboratory, teeming with outdoor exploration opportunities to observe wildlife and nature that includes mountain foothills, large tracts of forested lands, and expansive coastline, all within short drives of the UA campus. The city of Tuscaloosa is a vibrant, college town with daily Amtrak service to New Orleans, LA and Atlanta, GA.

Minimum Qualifications
A Ph.D. in Environmental Science, Earth Science, Physical Geography, or a closely related field is required at the time of appointment.

Contact information for three professional references. Review of applications will begin November 2026, and the search will continue until the position is filled. The expected start date of the position is August 16, 2027. Questions about the position can be directed to search committee chair, Professor Lisa Davis, [email removed].

Description


The Roadside Ecology Center (REC) at Southern Illinois University Carbondale invites applications for a Landscape Ecologist. This position provides technical and scientific leadership for the Center’s conservation planning, spatial prioritization, remote sensing, and ecological modeling activities. Working at the intersection of transportation infrastructure and landscape science, the Landscape Ecologist applies advanced geospatial tools and quantitative methods to determine where and how the effects of roads and land use on wildlife, habitats, and ecosystem processes can best be avoided, minimized, and mitigated across Illinois. The Landscape Ecologist works independently and collaboratively with field scientists, the GIS Manager, graduate research associates, and IDOT partners to design spatial analyses and modeling frameworks that translate field-collected data into landscape-scale conservation strategies. This position serves as the Center’s lead for identifying priority areas for mitigation investment, evaluating the effectiveness of conservation actions, and advancing the practice of road ecology through applied research and peer-reviewed publication.



Examples of Duties

Lead landscape-scale conservation planning and spatial prioritization efforts, identifying where mitigation investments and avoidance strategies will deliver the greatest ecological return. 
Design and conduct spatial analyses using remote sensing imagery, LiDAR, and land cover data to map habitat condition, model species distributions, assess landscape connectivity, and evaluate cumulative infrastructure effects across Illinois. 
Develop, adapt, and maintain ecological models and spatial decision-support tools that enable IDOT environmental planners to assess project-level impacts within a landscape context and prioritize conservation actions programmatically. 
Collaborate with field biologists, the GIS Manager, and graduate students to integrate field-collected occurrence and survey data into landscape models, ensuring that spatial prioritization frameworks are grounded in field-validated ecological conditions. 
Contribute to the design and implementation of Center research projects; prepare and publish findings in peer-reviewed journals and technical reports, and present results at professional conferences and to IDOT agency stakeholders. 
Support graduate research associates and, where applicable, interns or field technicians on spatial analysis methods, ecological modeling techniques, and scientific communication. 
Maintain current knowledge of emerging remote sensing technologies, machine learning applications, and best practices in landscape ecology, road ecology, and conservation planning.

Qualifications

Minimum Qualifications:
Master’s degree in landscape ecology, conservation biology, ecology, environmental science, geography, or a closely related field 
Minimum of three years of professional experience as a Landscape Ecologist and/or Spatial Planner. 
Demonstrated record of peer-reviewed publication in applied ecology or conservation biology, commensurate with the university-level Assistant Scientist classification 
Demonstrated proficiency with ArcGIS Pro and at least one ecological modeling or statistical platform (R, Python, Google Earth Engine, or equivalent).
Experience processing and analyzing remote sensing datasets, including multispectral imagery, LiDAR, or land cover products, for ecological applications. 
Experience conducting species distribution modeling, habitat suitability analysis, landscape connectivity modeling, or other landscape-scale prioritization methods. 
Strong technical writing skills with demonstrated ability to produce peer-reviewed publications or technical reports for agency audiences. 
Ability to work both independently and collaboratively within a multi-disciplinary team; valid driver’s license required.
Preferred Qualifications:
Ph.D. in landscape ecology, conservation biology, geography, or related field with a focus on spatial ecology or applied conservation planning, or five or more years of professional experience as a landscape ecologist in road ecology, transportation agency work, or environmental consulting. 
Familiarity with road ecology, transportation infrastructure impacts on wildlife, or landscape connectivity analysis in the context of linear infrastructure. 
Familiarity with decision science frameworks (e.g., structured decision-making) 
Knowledge of Illinois or Midwestern flora, fauna, and natural communities, particularly species of conservation concern. 
Familiarity with NEPA, ESA Section 7, or other environmental compliance frameworks relevant to transportation projects.
